articles.title: Stephen Miller pushed for 3,000 ICE arrests a day. Now he's Trump's chief of staff.
articles.summary: Washington — Top Trump adviser Stephen Miller , who is set to take over the White House chief of staff role on Monday, has driven President Trump's most controversial immigration policies during both of his administrations. Mr. Trump announced the staffing shake-up on Friday, calling Miller one of his "most trusted" advisers. Miller replaces Susie Wiles, who has been his chief of staff throughout his second term. The move comes after Republicans suffered crippling losses in the midterm elections and as Democrats plan sweeping investigations into the administration's actions, including its immigration enforcement policies. Miller was the architect behind many of those policies and also championed the administration's immigration enforcement expansion, which has been supported by approximately $170 billion that congressional Republicans allocated for immigration enforcement and border security in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which became law in July 2025. During Mr. Trump's first term, Miller helped develop and publicly defend the administration's executive order that restricted entry by nationals of several Muslim-majority countries. The travel ban led to protests around the U.S. and legal challenges. A third iteration of the ban was upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018. He was a leading supporter of the administration's 2018 zero-tolerance immigration policy, which resulted in thousands of family separations, and he pressed for dramatic reductions in refugee admissions. The administration repeatedly lowered the annual refugee admissions ceiling, ultimately setting it at 15,000 for fiscal year 2021, a record low at the time. Under former President Barack Obama, the ceiling was 110,000 for fiscal year 2017. Miller also advocated penalizing legal immigrants who received public benefits and making it harder for them to obtain citizenship. In Mr. Trump's second term, Miller pushed Immigration and Customs Enforcement to make at least 3,000 immigration arrests per day. In May 2025, Miller publicly demanded a dramatic increase in daily arrests, placing pressure on ICE leadership and expanding enforcement beyond immigrants who had been convicted of serious crimes. He also proposed that the National Guard be deployed to support mass deportations. Miller's arrest targets were part of a sweeping expansion of enforcement in communities, workplaces and immigration courts. Detentions of immigrants without criminal histories rose sharply , and increased ICE activity sparked protests across the country. The longtime Trump adviser also championed the use of a wartime law — the Alien Enemies Act of 1798 — to bypass due process and quickly deport alleged Venezuelan gang members to El Salvador, where they were held in a notorious maximum-security prison, known as CECOT. The deportations set off a legal battle, and the Supreme Court blocked the government from immediately deporting the Venezuelans without giving them an opportunity to challenge their removal. As part of the administration's deportation efforts, Miller has supported an aggressive expansion of third-country deportations . The administration has deported immigrants to countries where they have no citizenship or family ties, including several African nations . In May 2025, Miller said the administration was actively considering suspending the constitutional mechanism that allows detainees to challenge their confinement in court. At a March 2026 conference in Miami, Miller argued that military force, rather than traditional criminal law enforcement alone, was needed to defeat cartels. Miller appeared alongside Mr. Trump in the Oval Office this summer as he signed executive orders to refuse citizenship to some children born in the United States, after the Supreme Court struck down his earlier executive order aiming to end birthright citizenship. articles.title: The Trump admin wants underwater data centers. 1 non-profit is already preparing.
articles.summary: The skyline of Cleveland, Ohio, on 30 September 2023. Photograph: Photo by Mike Kline (notkalvin)/Getty Images While Elon Musk has often touted putting datacenters in space, reports suggest that another geographic area may soon become a widespread target: our lakes and oceans . Two underwater datacenters are already in operation off the coast of China, and recent reports suggest that the Trump administration is considering plans for four proposed underwater, sealed-pod datacenters to be built off the shores of Maine and Alaska . At a campaign rally in Ohio last month, Donald Trump said of datacenters: “There’s so much money to be made for Ohio … they’ll go to China … we want them.” Underwater iterations are particularly attractive to tech companies as they largely eliminate community opposition and controversy around datacenters in residential areas on land. In theory, underwater datacenters could also significantly cut down on utility costs, another issue that’s currently riling communities across the country. A Microsoft project set up off the coast of northern Scotland in 2018 found that after two years, server failures were reduced by 87% compared with on-land datacenter equivalents. Microsoft executives saw the project, which ended after two years, as an unmitigated success. That makes the cool, salt-free waters of the Great Lakes, home to 30 million people in major cities such as Chicago, Toronto and Detroit, potentially attractive to datacenter companies. A spokesperson for the federal Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said: “The EPA supports development of data center infrastructure that is essential to remaining the world leader in Super Intelligence while using its statutory authorities to protect water quality.” But the environmental consequences of any similar project in the freshwater Great Lakes, which those tens of millions of people depend on for drinking water every day, could be significant. Local environmental activists are already worried and sounding the alarm – even though no underwater datacenter projects are currently proposed for the region. For them, they think it is better to be prepared than surprised, given the high stakes of the ecologically sensitive ecosystem. “We are concerned because if you think about what a datacenter does, it throws off a lot of heat. Lake Erie already has an issue with harmful algal blooms, and they develop because of heat, not only because of fertilizers and agricultural runoff,” said John Lipaj of the Lake Erie Foundation , a non-profit based in Ohio. The floor of Lake Erie on the US side falls under the jurisdiction of the state of Ohio. In the past, its state government, where Republicans hold a supermajority, proposed a law making it easier for datacenter companies to discharge wastewater into public waterways. That measure was denied by the state’s EPA last July following a public outcry. Of the eight US Great Lakes states, only New York currently has a temporary state-wide moratorium on datacenter construction. That ends in mid-2027. “We’re also concerned about the possibility of contamination and leaks. These have not been around a long time,” said Lipaj. “We are concerned about the types of fluid contained in a datacenter, the batteries and electrical equipment. These are all things that could lead to a catastrophic failure that we don’t want happening in the Great Lakes.” Lake Erie is home or close to major cities such as Cleveland, Detroit and Buffalo and is already by far the warmest of the five Great Lakes during summer months. It also ranks as one of the most polluted large lakes in the country in large part due to agricultural runoff in its western basin. A number of fish species are under threat due to the lake’s warming trend. “Warm water can impact aquatic life and ecosystems in a number of ways. One immediate effect is what is known as a thermal shock,” said Helena Volzer of the Alliance for the Great Lakes, an environmental group based in Chicago. “Aquatic organisms are highly sensitive to temperature changes, and even a small, rapid increase of just 2-5F can be dramatic for the aquatic ecosystem. When a facility releases warm water, it can alter metabolism and increase oxygen demand, reduce dissolved oxygen availability, disrupt food webs [and] force fish to move away from preferred habitats.” On 3 November, residents of Conneaut, a Lake Erie community of about 12,000 people an hour’s drive north-east of Cleveland, voted in favor of a charter amendment to prohibit the construction of large datacenters in its area. But the idea of offshore underwater datacenters is not a popular one here. “Being one of the largest freshwater sources in the world, I would be very much for protecting that resource,” said Mariana Branch, a Conneaut council member who lives a short distance from the Lake Erie shoreline. Branch said she hadn’t previously been aware of the idea of datacenters operating underwater. “Technology is moving so quickly, it’s difficult for cities to keep up with,” she said. Still, some suggest that following Microsoft’s lead in Scotland may have some merit considering the public opposition to on-land equivalents; and, unlike the open ocean, there are no large fauna in the Great Lakes ecosystems. “They require a lot of energy for cooling … one of the biggest advantages of these underwater datacenters is the low cooling cost [associated]. They don’t have to spend a lot to cool the servers,” said Nir Kshetri, a professor of emerging technologies at the University of North Carolina Greensboro. “Datacenters have been a big issue for communities and in the recent elections. Also, datacenters don’t have to worry about any latency problems because they can be located close to large population centers where they are needed. A lake is a great place to do a datacenter. Cold water is even better.” However, the Great Lakes are not without significant challenges to any such project. Last winter saw one of the most extensive Great Lakes freeze-ups in decades, with almost all of Lake Erie and up to half of the four other lakes freezing over up to several feet deep. Experts say it isn’t clear to what extent ice cover could affect underwater projects. What’s more, a Microsoft spokesperson said: “We have no plans to deploy an underwater datacenter in any location at this time,” and: “Our focus today is on building and operating datacenters responsibly on land.” A spokesperson for Ohio’s EPA said it had not yet received any applications to permit an underwater datacenter in its part of Lake Erie. For its part, Lipaj says the Lake Erie Foundation has contacted state representatives and state senators in New York, Ohio and Michigan to discuss the issue. “Whether or not they happen, [we’re saying] let’s propose to state legislatures in Great Lakes states that they consider that this may be coming down the line and let’s get some regulations in place before the datacenter developers make their proposals and then state legislators are scrambling. That’s what we’re trying to avoid. We’re exercising an abundance of caution,” he said. “The Great Lakes states should take some leadership in this, get the regulations written so that nothing is forced on them.” This article originally appeared on The Guardian at https://www.yahoo.com/news/us/articles/trump-administration-wants-underwater-datacenters-140014506.html

articles.title: House Democrats will start their majority focused on healthcare and ending the Iran war
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democratic leaders are placing an early emphasis on healthcare as they discuss their immediate priorities upon the swearing-in of the new Congress on Jan. 3. Early votes in the House next year are expected to focus on boosting Medicaid and restoring an enhanced tax subsidy that is designed to lower the cost of Affordable Care Act health plans for millions of enrollees . Democrats are also promising swift action on legislation to stop the war with Iran and to reverse some of President Donald Trump's trade tariffs . “We’re going to get out of the gate fast,” said New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic leader who is in line to become the next House speaker . The legislative flurry carries enormous stakes for Democrats as they seek to translate their sweeping victories in the midterms — their numbers will exceed 250 in the 435-member House — into achievements that deliver on their promises to lower the cost of living. Obstacles abound for the Democratic agenda Passing those bills should not be a problem with such a large Democratic House majority . Getting them signed into law most certainly could be. A 60-vote threshold in the Senate looms for the legislation, as does a potential presidential veto. Trump on election night posted a photo on his social media site of a red hat with a simple message on it: “VETO”. Following those early votes, Jeffries said five working groups are developing plans to put forward bills that would lower costs in areas such as housing, energy, groceries and caregiving. Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif., said Democrats will at some point take up legislation dealing with artificial intelligence and data centers. He is part of a group of lawmakers working on a document that will lay out some of the priorities for Jeffries to consider. “House Republicans last year made a conscious decision to let the AI industry run wild, and that was a bad decision politically and a bad decision on policy,” Lieu said. “Two things will change next term. We will hold public hearings on AI. We will pass legislation, reasonable guardrails on AI, and specifically data centers.” New Congress will return to past political fights Democrats are trying to reverse Medicaid changes that are expected to cut more than $900 billion from the program over a decade. The Republican-approved cuts helped offset some of the costs of Trump's big tax and spending cut bill that was signed into law last year. The Medicaid changes in the bill imposed new administrative requirements and added conditions for eligibility, including work requirements. Some of the most substantial changes have yet to take effect. Still, enrollment in Medicaid has dropped by about 5 million, or about 7% since July 2025, when the bill was signed into law, according to KFF, a health policy research and news organization. Reversing those cuts would likely require Trump and the Republicans to abandon the hard-fought changes they made to cut entitlement spending in their signature tax bill. It's an unlikely proposition. The effort to extend enhanced tax subsidies for certain enrollees in ACA plans has also been debated and voted on in the current Congress. The measure passed the House with some Republican support but stalled in the Senate. There also have been numerous war powers votes regarding Iran — 14 in the Senate and six in the House. Gridlock may be on the horizon Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said going into the election that a Democratic majority in the next Congress would amount to “two years of paralysis.” “I don’t think that’s good for anybody,” Thune said. But Democratic leader Chuck Schumer of New York is insisting that Democrats will push their agenda with or without the Republican president's help. “If he vetoes it, it will show the divisions. As much as we didn’t want to shut down, when we shut down the government for a month over healthcare , people knew we were on their side,” Schumer said in an interview with The New York Times' podcast “The Daily.” Schumer said he believes Democrats can gain some Republican votes on restoring the enhanced subsidies for ACA plans. When asked if he was hearing from Republicans expressing a willingness to work with him on legislation, he replied: “They’re never so definitive but, yes, I am getting initial signs that way on certain issues, not on every issue.” While the prospects for getting any of the early priority bills over the finish line are uncertain, the votes in Congress will help frame the choices voters will face during a presidential election in 2028. Tensions exist within the new Democratic majority Progressive groups call the agenda outlined by Jeffries a good early start, but they have much greater expectations for Democrats this Congress. “It's perfectly fine if the Senate and the House are unified and Donald Trump is standing in the way because that sets up another tidal wave election in 2028,” said Adam Green, co-founder of the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, a Democratic-aligned group that backs progressive candidates and policies. At the same time, he said Schumer cannot be content to let bills die in the Senate because of the 60-vote threshold. “It will require the Democrats to get rid of the filibuster,” Green said. “There's no doubt about it.” He said there's a disparity because Republicans' top priorities — tax cuts and Supreme Court justices — can get through with simple majorities. But the Democratic Party's top priorities require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. “The only question is will the American public trust Democrats enough to keep giving us more power or will this week's gains whittle away because we do nothing? That's why the filibuster is a threshold question," Green said. Schumer in an interview with The Associated Press this week would not say whether he would try and eliminate the filibuster. “The focus has got to be on getting things done,” Schumer said. “That’s all I am saying.” In a memo to fellow members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Rep. Greg Casar, D-Texas, said Democrats also need to target what he called “powerful forces outside of government.” Examples he cited were corporations using Americans’ private data to adjust their pricing based on a consumer's personal data and AI companies that he says are putting jobs and lives at risk. "By focusing not just on the Trump administration but also on big corporations and billionaires, we will show the American people we are not just anti-Trump but also pro-worker and pro-consumer," Casar said. ___ Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed to this report. articles.title: Trump's grip on his party is in question as Republicans reel from the midterm wipeout
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — Republicans aren't holding back. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis described this week's elections as an “extinction-level event” for the GOP. Texas Sen. Ted Cruz likened it to a “Watergate-level repudiation.” Former Vice President Mike Pence called it a “reckoning.” For all the apocalyptic talk emerging from a midterm that relegated Republicans to their thinnest ranks on Capitol Hill in decades, there's little agreement on how the party should move forward. A return to the bedrock fiscal and national security conservatism that defined Republicans under President Ronald Reagan risks alienating the more hard-line conservatives welcomed into the party under President Donald Trump under the “Make America Great Again” banner. But leaning even further into Trump's coarse brand of politics could lead to more voter rejection. “We have soul-searching to do," Alex Latcham, the executive director of the Senate Leadership Fund, which spent $810 million to support Republicans, said in an interview. “We need to first understand and honestly admit why we just endured a wipeout of this magnitude. And then we have to regroup and agree to a path forward.” GOP faces questions about Trump's future role As has been the case for the past decade, the central question is the role Trump will play in shaping the party's future. His insistence on loyalty reached a zenith this year as he intervened in GOP primaries and pressed voters to make the elections a referendum on his second term. He held dozens of rallies in the final weeks of the campaign for candidates, most of whom lost their races. Since Tuesday's election, he's refused to acknowledge any responsibility, placing blame on the candidates. His public events have focused on his pet projects in Washington, which have proven unpopular with voters. On Friday, he elevated Stephen Miller , the architect of some of his most contentious policies, to White House chief of staff. In an interview, Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt , a Republican, said the election results were “shocking” but that Trump could still steer the conversation around issues such as immigration. The governor described the GOP's current dynamic as a natural process for a party whose leader is deep in his second term. “It just tells you that the American people, after 10 years, they're pretty much tired of whoever's in office,” Stitt said. “I think people want a little more stability. They want people to be nice to people, to say, 'Hey, we’re all Americans.'” Others were more blunt. Longtime conservative commentator Tucker Carlson said the midterms marked “the end of the Trump era." John Sununu, a Republican who lost his bid for a Senate seat in New Hampshire, blamed Trump. "It seems like he or his family is in on every transaction and deal that goes on in Washington,” Sununu told John Kasich, a former Republican congressman from Ohio, on SiriusXM. “Those two things, I think, caused people to say, ‘You know, I just can’t vote for a Republican while he’s still in office.’” Republican infighting is likely to intensify The GOP infighting is poised to intensify quickly. When Republicans return to Capitol Hill next week, they'll have to choose between Reps. Steve Scalise of Louisiana and Jim Jordan of Ohio to lead the party in the House. They may weigh whether to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . There could also be tough votes on defense spending and keeping the federal government open after Dec. 11. Already a leadership fight is brewing at the Republican National Committee, where there are early conversations about limiting Trump’s influence in picking the next chair. KC Crosbie, currently the co-chair, circulated a letter this week calling the midterms a “serious setback” and announcing plans to run for chair at the committee’s January meeting in Arizona. Trump announced his support Friday for the party's current chair, Joe Gruters. That's to say nothing of the emerging contest for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination. Vice President JD Vance , seen as a leading contender, will likely face a broad range of opponents if he enters the race. Stitt is among the Republicans calling for a “big open primary.” “I don't think we should crown anybody,” he said. There will be pressure to revive the coalition of voters, particularly Latinos, who have lifted the party to success in previous elections but swung to Democrats this week. Former Rep. Carlos Curbelo, R-Fla., said he thought Secretary of State Marco Rubio is best positioned to win Latinos. “The two main constituencies that Republicans have to quickly regain are white suburban voters and Hispanic voters,” Curbelo said in an interview. “Vance was out on the campaign trail this year and it doesn't appear that he was able to move the needle in terms of Hispanic voters.” A representative for Vance didn't comment on that characterization. Broad election fallout for the GOP Still, the fallout for the GOP is broad, according to The AP Voter Poll , an expansive survey of about 80,000 voters in all 50 states. Younger Republican voters who supported the Republican candidate in their House race were less likely to approve of the way Trump is handling his job as president, and more likely to say he worsened the economy with his policies. About two-thirds of Republican voters under 30 said they approved of how Trump was handling the presidency, compared with about 9 in 10 Republican voters age 65 and older. About one-third of younger GOP voters said Trump had worsened the country’s economic conditions, compared with about 2 in 10 older Republican voters. The war with Iran also appeared to divide Republican voters, with about 6 in 10 Republican voters under 45 saying the U.S. made the right decision in taking military action against Iran. That rose to about 8 in 10 among Republican voters who were 45 and older. Young Republican voters were more likely to say the U.S. support for Israel was “too strong.” Roughly half of Republican voters under 30 said the country’s backing of Israel was “too strong,” compared with about 1 in 10 voters 65 and older. Despite rosy outlooks from top Republicans including Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in the final weeks of the campaign, Republican strategists had long seen the country's confidence in the party unraveling. In late August, the Senate Leadership Fund convened a donor retreat in Laguna Beach, California, where Latcham told the group that Republicans had lost the confidence of voters on handling the cost of living and the economy, according to two Republican Senate campaign sources who attended the event. They spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a private meeting. In defeat, Republicans are trying to take a broader view, knowing that it may take several election cycles before they one day return to power. Rep. Christopher Smith was reelected to his 24th term this week and is New Jersey's last Republican in Congress. He took a long view on the party's current struggles. “The pendulum swings back and forth,” he told reporters. “These are cycles.” ___ Associated Press writers Steve Peoples, Kevin Freking and Linley Sanders contributed to this report. articles.title: The warming impacts of El Niño are forecast to delay the onset of winter
articles.summary: Widespread chilly weather still seems a long way away despite what the calendar says, as the nation is forecast to see one of the warmest Novembers on record, thanks mainly to the warming impacts of El Niño , forecasters said. "The ongoing El Niño remains the dominant teleconnection to influence this forecast (for November)," said Johnna Infanti, a forecaster from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center , in an online report . Chad Merrill, a senior meteorologist from AccuWeather , told USA TODAY that "a very warm month is expected nationally. It will likely rank in the top 10 for warmest Novembers." Where are above-average temperatures expected in November? The temperature forecast map from the Climate Prediction Center (above) shows orange for nearly the entire nation, meaning above-average temperatures are likely practically coast-to-coast. On the map, only the Southwest is not forecast to see above-normal temperatures. In the Southwest, there are "equal chances" of seeing warmer-than-average or cooler-than-average temperatures. No part of the U.S. is forecast to see below-average temperatures this month. Specifically, Merrill told USA TODAY that "Northern California into the Northwest into the northern portion of the Plains through the Mississippi Valley and into the East will be warmer than the historical average for temperatures." Which areas are forecast to see above-average precipitation in November? According to the Climate Prediction Center map, the wettest parts of the nation in November will be the Southwest and the central and northern Plains. The only states that should see a drier-than-average November are Michigan and Montana, the CPC map shows. AccuWeather also said that Southern California coastal flooding remains a concern: Coastal flooding is expected to continue into November, with some of the highest coastal water levels of the season forecast to occur around Nov. 25, AccuWeather said. Are there any major storms in the forecast? "Our long-range team expects at least one sizable storm to bring copious snow to the Mountain West and heavy rain that will trigger some flooding to the West, particularly California, the Great Basin and Southwest," Merrill said. In the East, Merrill said there will likely be a storm closer to Thanksgiving week that brings heavy rain to the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic states. Thanksgiving weekend could bring a taste of winter, AccuWeather said. Colder air could bring flurries or snow to parts of the Great Lakes and Northeast. What's causing this mild pattern across much of the nation? "A highly energized Pacific jet stream triggered by both the strong El Niño and marine heat waves in the Pacific are flooding much of the U.S. with warmer-than-average temperatures in November," Merrill told USA TODAY. Looking ahead to December and beyond, the warmth is expected to continue, as El Niño tends to make winters warmer in the U.S., especially across the northern half of the nation. This is due to unusually warm water temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean, which shifts the jet stream and makes extended invasions of cold, Arctic air less likely to occur. Doyle Rice is a national correspondent for USA TODAY, with a focus on weather and climate. This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: When will winter weather arrive? articles.title: Newsom's death penalty gamble could help him in 2028 — or come back to bite him
articles.summary: A view of the East Block of San Quentin Rehab Center's death row, which was shut down by Gov. Gavin Newsom earlier in his term before he announced Thursday that he was commuting the sentences of condemned inmates. (Robert Gauthier / Los Angeles Times) While running for California governor in 2018, Gavin Newsom declared that he would rather be bold and fail than retreat to the safety of mediocrity. The two-term governor known for taking big political risks once again made good on that vow Thursday when he moved to offer clemency to every inmate sentenced to death in California. Amid a hum of speculation about how the mass commutation could help or hurt his presidential prospects in 2028, the Democratic politician sent a clear, defining message to Americans about where he stands and the type of leader they could expect. “If my job is just to read the polls, you can have an AI chatbot as governor,” Newsom said in an interview Friday. “I was hired for my judgment, and like it or hate it, that was why I think I was given this privilege, and that’s the responsibility of a leader. My job’s leadership, not stewardship. It’s not management. It’s to lead. “I’m here to change polls, change minds.” The sweeping decision comes more than 20 years after Newsom emerged in the national consciousness when, as mayor of San Francisco, he defied federal law and allowed same-sex marriages in the City by the Bay. California Gov. Gavin Newsom speaks at the "Stop the Power Grab rally" at the Hollywood Palladium in Los Angeles on Nov. 1, 2026. (Ariana Drehsler / For The Times) Bold moves that test the limits of his power, such as a controversial, first-in-the-nation stay-at-home order during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic and spearheading Proposition 50 last year to redraw California’s congressional districts to offset Republican attempts to gerrymander red states, have defined his leadership, for good or bad. The Democratic governor said those kinds of decisions are “sort of embedded in my DNA.” About a decade ago he said he was pushed to describe his core motivation. Though he admits it sounds trite, the governor said: “It’s to stand up for ideals and strike out against injustice.” The death penalty, he said, is not handed out equally. He quoted Bryan Stevenson, the founder of Equal Justice Initiative, who said you’re better off being rich and guilty than poor and innocent. “I couldn’t not have done this,” Newsom said. “There was an easy out, but ... I would the rest of my life felt, you know, ashamed of myself.” Commuting the death sentences of all 548 state prisoners awaiting execution pushes the bounds of his authority once again. California voters have twice rejected ballot measures to abolish the death penalty , first in 2012 and again in 2016, and Newsom’s decision overrides the will of the courts and state laws that permit capital punishment. Read more: Newsom moves to commute all California death sentences to life in prison without parole Under the state Constitution, Newsom has the power    to commute about 40% of the death sentences on his own. The rest of the cases, which involve prisoners who had a felony conviction on their record prior to receiving a death sentence, or racked up additional crimes while awaiting execution, require approval from the California Supreme Court — a constitutional check to ensure the governor’s actions are not an abuse of power. The court rejected 10 commutations handed out by Gov. Jerry Brown in his last full month in office — all of which involved people convicted of multiple felonies — and did not provide an explanation for the action. Despite Newsom’s push to commute all death sentences, capital punishment remains legal in California and prosecutors can continue seeking that punishment. Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman speaks during a news conference at the Hall of Justice last month. (Ronaldo Bolaños / Los Angeles Times) Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan Hochman said until the law is changed, his office “will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand.” Sacramento County Sheriff Jim Cooper urged Newsom to reconsider the commutations. He said he remembers watching Luis Bracamontes, who was sentenced to death for killing Sacramento County Sheriff’s Deputy Danny Oliver and Placer County Sheriff’s Detective Michael Davis Jr. in 2014, “laugh in court while their families, including Danny’s two young daughters, had to sit and watch. “Deputy Danny Oliver and Detective Michael Davis Jr. should be alive today, enjoying long and healthy lives with their families,” Cooper said in a statement. “Instead, the man who murdered them has now escaped his sentence.” Others accused the governor of reducing the death penalty sentences to seek an advantage in the 2028 presidential election. “The people of California deserve leaders who put politics and personal ambition aside and pursue truth, accountability, and justice with courage, integrity, and transparency,” said Michael Hestrin, Riverside County district attorney, in a statement. “Instead they have been presented with a decision that demonstrates a profound disregard for the victims, their families, and the prosecutors who dedicated themselves to seeking justice on their behalf.” Luis Bracamontes looks up in Sacramento Superior Court in 2018 as the verdict is read in the killing of two law enforcement officers. Bracamontes was found guilty. (Rich Pedroncelli / Associated Press) A poll conducted in August by the Pew Research Center found that about two-thirds of voters nationally favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder. Political analysts suggest that reducing the sentences adds to Newsom’s credentials as a progressive leader and aligns him with Democratic primary voters on the issue if he runs for president. Republicans, however, could take advantage of Newsom’s action and cast him as a soft-on-crime liberal who is out of touch with most Americans, which risks turning away moderate voters. But others cautioned that national political elections are hard to predict. Gar Culbert, chair of the political science department at Cal State Los Angeles, said it would be politically advantageous for Newsom to try to appeal to the Democratic  Party’s base as he considers a run for president. Culbert said he doesn’t believe the death penalty will be a substantial issue in a general election when, if Newsom becomes the Democratic presidential nominee, his Republican challenger would attack his record as California governor regardless. “It’s possible he’s not being strategic,” Culbert said. “Maybe he doesn’t have to be strategic because he just might think it’s the right thing to do.” The governor first issued a moratorium on executions about two months after he took office in 2019, saying capital punishment is discriminatory and unjust. Without the moratorium, 45 people would be subject to execution now, according to his office. Daniel Zingale worked for Newsom as a senior advisor in the governor’s office at the start of his first term. Part of Zingale’s job at the time was to consider how the governor’s actions would be received by the public. “The only piece of data he was not interested in in that process were the polls,” Zingale said. “His view, and I agree with this, is this is not an issue that you can leverage politically.” Read more: Gov. Gavin Newsom to block California death row executions, close San Quentin execution chamber Newsom’s decision to commute the sentences won’t have much practical effect in a state that has not executed a prisoner since 2006. At Newsom’s command, the death chamber was dismantled at San Quentin State Prison, now San Quentin Rehabilitation Center, after he issued his moratorium. His successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, has also said he will continue the pause on executions. There was no immediate need to offer commutations to save the lives of the inmates. Taking no action would have been the safe bet, Newsom said in an interview about his decision a day after he made the announcement. Many people around him, he said, advised him to do nothing. He also understands that commuting the sentences could make him vulnerable if he runs for president. “I’m not an idiot. The ads write themselves,” Newsom said. “But I just also would be fake. I wouldn’t be myself and if I’m going to be up there and not be myself, I couldn’t do that.” With the clock ticking on his time in office, the governor said he also doesn’t want to leave with regrets. “I don’t want to be one of the elders on some panel talking about what I would have, could have, should have done,” Newsom said. “I’ve spent my life trying not to be that person. I’ve been willing to take risks. I’ve been willing to go first on so many issues. “If others aren’t willing to do it, you know what? I’ll raise my hand, and I’m happy, honestly, to take the hits.” Sign up for Essential California for news, features and recommendations from the L.A. Times and beyond in your inbox six days a week. articles.title: Trump signals more cabinet changes in store after Republican midterm losses
articles.summary: Hegseth and Miller (AP) President Donald Trump said Friday he expects to make additional Cabinet changes following Republicans' sweeping midterm election defeats, signaling that the replacement of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles may be only the beginning of a broader administration shake-up. In an interview with CBS News' "60 Minutes," Trump acknowledged that more personnel changes could be coming but declined to identify which officials might be affected. Asked whether he expected to fire anyone after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress, Trump replied, "I do, yeah. Little bit." "I love my Cabinet. I think they're good," Trump said. "But I'll ... be doing maybe a few changes." The remarks came as Trump announced Friday that longtime senior adviser Stephen Miller would replace Wiles as White House chief of staff, effective Monday. Trump's comments were made during an interview with CBS News correspondent Ross Douthat scheduled to air Sunday, with excerpts released Friday. The president's remarks also come amid growing speculation about the future of War Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose handling of the war in Iran has drawn criticism following the GOP's midterm losses. CBS News reported Wednesday that Trump had privately asked advisers whether Hegseth should remain in his position, citing multiple sources familiar with the discussions. The network reported that Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis had been floated as a possible replacement, although other sources said Trump had made no decision to remove Hegseth. Trump publicly expressed confidence in Hegseth when questioned Wednesday and again during the CBS interview. "I do," Trump replied Friday when asked whether he retained confidence in Hegseth. "Look, we've won two wars," the president added, referring to U.S. military operations in Venezuela and Iran. Hegseth also faces the prospect of intensified congressional scrutiny when Democrats take control of the House and Senate in January. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., said Friday that Hegseth should leave office but stopped short of endorsing impeachment proceedings, according to NPR. "He's got to go," Jeffries said during an interview with NPR's "Morning Edition." Asked whether Democrats should pursue impeachment, Jeffries replied, "I don't want to get out ahead of the caucus." NPR also reported that Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., has threatened to force a House vote on eight articles of impeachment unless Hegseth resigns. Meanwhile, Trump's decision to elevate Miller places one of his closest advisers in charge of White House operations as Democrats prepare to challenge administration policies and launch congressional investigations. CBS News reported Friday that Miller, previously deputy chief of staff, has played a central role in shaping Trump's immigration enforcement and deportation policies. His appointment could also set the stage for a more confrontational relationship with incoming Democrat congressional leaders, who have sharply criticized the administration's immigration agenda. Trump, however, rejected suggestions that Wiles' departure was prompted by the election results. "It's just time. Sometimes you change," Trump told reporters Friday, according to CNN. CBS News separately reported that Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday and that her departure was tied to the Republican election defeats, citing three sources familiar with the matter. Trump praised Miller as a trusted and effective adviser. "He's been with me right from the beginning ... he's very loyal, smart. Does a great job," Trump said, according to CNN. "He's been an MVP every year. He's been just great. So, we're very happy with him," the president added. Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, has specifically identified Miller as a target for investigation. "Oversight Democrats will continue to investigate Miller for his misconduct," Garcia said in a statement Friday reported by Mediaite. "Stephen Miller should lawyer up," Garcia added. CBS News also reported that Garcia had singled out Miller and other administration officials as potential investigative targets following Tuesday's elections. The White House has dismissed the prospect of such inquiries as politically motivated. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told CBS News. © 2026 Newsmax. articles.title: Man found parked near White House with multiple firearms, authorities say
articles.summary: A Venezuelan national was arrested after being found sitting in a stolen vehicle near the White House with several firearms, according to a criminal complaint and the Department of Homeland Security. The suspect, Ronny Guanipa-Chrinos, allegedly threatened to kill President Donald Trump, according to DHS. A Secret Service officer on patrol spotted the vehicle parked on Constitution Avenue, near the White House complex, shortly before midnight on Thursday, according to the complaint affidavit filed in D.C. Superior Court. Man arrested for alleged threats to shoot President Trump at Kansas rally When the officer knocked on the window of the blue Ford F-150 and asked if he was OK and whether he had any weapons, Guanipa-Chrinos allegedly shook his head yes and made a finger gun gesture, according to the affidavit. After getting out of the vehicle, he allegedly told investigators through Google Translate, "I have the gun because they tried to kill me with it, and I had to take it away from them; it's in the brown bag," according to the affidavit. According to DHS, Guanipa-Chrinos told officers he "heard voices in his head telling him to come to Washington, D.C. and kill President Trump." The affidavit did not include those alleged remarks. Department of Homeland Security - PHOTO: Firearms seized from a vehicle near the White House on Nov. 5, 2026, according to the Department of Homeland Security. Investigators found a MAC-10 machine pistol, a Glock 43x pistol and an AR-15 rifle in the vehicle, according to the affidavit. There were also "dozens of rounds of ammunition," DHS said. The vehicle had been reported stolen, according to the affidavit. Guanipa-Chrinos has been charged with unauthorized use of a vehicle, receiving stolen property, carrying a pistol without a license, carrying a rifle without a license and other firearms charges. He made an initial appearance in D.C. Superior Court on Friday and remains held without bond, according to online court records. Guanipa-Chrinos is undocumented and entered the U.S. through Texas in 2024, according to DHS. articles.title: Latino vote helped thwart Texas Republicans' redistricting effort
articles.summary: Last year, the Republican-controlled Texas legislature redrew its congressional maps in a controversial mid-decade redistricting effort aimed at giving the GOP five more House seats. Encouraged by President Donald Trump's strong showing among Hispanic voters in 2024, they concentrated on four districts in the heavily Latino Rio Grande Valley in South Texas. But the Latino vote in Texas swung back from the president on Tuesday, driven by its dissatisfaction with Trump's immigration policy and the economy, according to ABC News' Voter Poll. Republicans failed to flip any of the Rio Grand Valley districts -- losing by double-digits in all of them -- and ended up with a net loss of one House seat. Hispanic voters comprise more than 30% of eligible Texas voters and are especially concentrated in four counties in the Rio Grande Valley, where they make up more than 90% of the population, according to U.S. census data. Brandon Bell/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democrats candidate for House Bobby Pulido, Senate candidate James Talarico and gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa sing together at the conclusion of the Voto Latino's "Ready. Go. Vote." campaign rally, Oct. 25, 2026 in Weslaco, Texas. ABC News' Voter Poll showed 67% of Hispanics who voted in the state's Senate race said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement have gone too far, compared to 45% of white Senate voters. Who won the redistricting war? So far, it looks like Democrats Jon Taylor, a University of Texas at San Antonio political science professor, told ABC affiliate KSAT that this issue is especially influential in the Rio Grande Valley saying, "A number of people living in South Texas, living in San Antonio, who had family, friends, somebody they knew who got picked up in an ICE raid. It had a profound impact on voting." About 83% of Hispanic voters said the economy was not so good or poor, compared to 63% of white voters, according to ABC News' Voter Poll, and 75% of Hispanics who voted in the Senate race said that Trump's economic policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., compared to 52% of white voters. The Rio Grande Valley has some of the highest rates of poverty in the country. Héctor E. Sánchez Barba, who leads Mi Familia Vota, a leading Latino political group, told ABC News that the Valley has been particularly hurt by the Trump's economic policies, saying "It's very clear the economic impact that these policies are having is on mostly working-class, people-of-color communities." All four of the Rio Grande Valley counties saw voter turnout up from 2022: Up 9.9% in Hidalgo County; 7.9% higher in Cameron County; a 7.4% increase in Willacy County; and 3.3% higher in Starr County. The state saw an overall increase of about 6% in voter turnout from 2022. Brandon Bell/Getty Images - PHOTO: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico speaks during a campaign rally at the Santa Fe Event Center, Oct. 25, 2026, in Weslaco, Texas. Additionally, Democrats flipped two largely Hispanic districts in South Texas that Trump had previously won by double digit margins. And the blue wave extended to Democrats winning all statewide races. ABC News Voter polls showed that Hispanic voters backed Democratic Senate Candidate James Talarico with 68% of the vote and Democratic governor candidate Gina Hinojosa with 65%. Barba said they won because "Their policies are a reflection of working class families" and a "reflection of inclusion." Barba said the Democratic victories could make the state a presidential battleground in 2028. "Make no mistake, anybody that wants to become a president in 2028 has to come through the Latino community." articles.title: Democrats' midterm wins could change how we elect presidents by 2028
articles.summary: Could this year's big blue midterm wave transform how America elects its next president? Now that Democrats have won complete control of governor's mansions and both legislative chambers in five battleground states — Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Nevada and Arizona — there is a chance that the Electoral College, as we know it, could soon become a thing of the past. That isn't speculation. In fact, the plan is already in motion. Over the last two decades, 18 states and Washington, D.C., have formally agreed to award all of their electoral votes to whichever presidential ticket wins the most votes nationwide, regardless of the outcome in their own state or district. Until now, this legal agreement — official name: the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) — hasn't taken effect because the jurisdictions that have joined it only control 222 total electoral votes, which falls short of the 270 required to activate the compact (and elect a president). But what if you add Pennsylvania (19 electoral votes), Michigan (15), Arizona (11), Wisconsin (10) and Nevada (6) to the list? That gets you to 283 (assuming that all of them join and the compact survives potential constitutional challenges). Since Election Day, the Democratic shift in statehouses across the country has been overshadowed by the massive Democratic shift on Capitol Hill . But as the dust settles, attention is turning toward a new possibility: that a handful of states might suddenly have the power to ensure that whoever wins the national popular vote in 2028 will also win the presidency (which hasn't always been the case ). "The time is right," Carrie Rheingans, a Democrat in the Michigan House of Representatives, told the New York Times this week . "This blue tsunami is really going to help push this forward across the whole nation." "National popular vote will be something that we'll prioritize early in the session," added Kelda Roys, a Democratic state lawmaker in Wisconsin. Here's everything you need to know about the national popular vote compact — and its chances of taking effect. How does the Electoral College currently work? The Electoral College is a system of indirect democracy in which the winner of the U.S. presidential election is determined not by the combined number of votes a candidate has earned across all states — aka the "popular vote" — but rather by the number of "electoral votes" they've amassed by winning in individual states. With minor exceptions, the candidate who gets the most votes in a particular state on Election Day is awarded all of that state's electoral votes, which match the number of senators and representatives it sends to Congress. Whichever presidential ticket secures a majority of electoral votes — that is, 270 — wins. Due to the winner-take-all nature of the Electoral College, candidates tend not to campaign in states that consistently vote Democratic (blue states) or Republican (red states). Instead, they focus on the small number of states (known as swing states, battleground states, toss-up states or purple states) that could go one way or the other. The Founding Fathers established the Electoral College in the Constitution. Some of them wanted qualified citizens to elect the president by popular vote; others wanted Congress to elect the president. The Electoral College was the compromise they landed on. Today's Electoral College system evolved over time as individual states passed their own winner-take-all laws. But the Founders never specified how electors — the ones who cast the electoral votes — would be appointed. Instead, the Constitution explicitly delegates that power to the states themselves, saying they can choose their electors "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct." National popular vote advocates argue that this clause gives state lawmakers " a built-in way to reform the system ." How could the national popular vote compact change America's presidential elections? Prior to the 20th century, three presidents won the White House without winning the popular vote: John Quincy Adams in 1824, Rutherford B. Hayes in 1876 and Benjamin Harrison in 1888. But the idea for a national popular vote compact only started to gain traction among scholars after George W. Bush lost the popular vote in 2000 and wound up in the White House anyway. Sixteen years later, Trump's popular-vote loss to Hillary Clinton — by a margin of nearly 3 million ballots — added more fuel to the fire. The Bush and Trump victories also polarized the issue, making Democrats more open to the idea of reform — and Republicans more opposed (in general). The NPVIC was introduced in 2006 by John Koza , a computer scientist and former Democratic elector who co-invented the lottery scratchcard. The idea is simple. First, individual states agree to award all of their electoral votes to the winner of the national popular vote. When enough states agree — that is, enough states with a combined total of at least 270 electoral votes — then the compact will take effect and the candidate who earns the most popular votes nationwide will be guaranteed enough electoral votes to win the White House. No constitutional amendment required. National popular vote proponents say that their plan will completely change the way candidates campaign for (and even govern as) president. Rather than lavishing all their time, energy and resources on a small handful of swing states, aspiring commanders in chief would in theory have to cater to voters everywhere in hopes of maximizing their nationwide vote tally. In April 2007, Maryland became the first state to sign on. Ten more jurisdictions followed suit before the 2016 election (California, Hawaii, Illinois, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington and the District of Columbia), with another eight joining the compact after Trump became president (Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Maine, Minnesota, New Mexico, Oregon and Virginia). Republican-led chambers have adopted the NPVIC in New York (2011), Oklahoma (2014) and Arizona (2016) — but generally, Democrats have needed complete statehouse control to enact it into law. Which is where Democrats' shiny new trifectas in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Arizona, Wisconsin and Nevada come into play. What's next According to the Times, "lawmakers in key states said on Thursday that they had already begun having conversations this week about introducing legislation to join the agreement in the next session, and were hopeful that they would succeed ahead of 2028." But hopeful doesn't mean certain. One of the new trifecta states, Michigan, failed to get over the line during its previous Democratic trifecta, from 2023 to 2024 — and Nevada fell short in 2019 when its then-Democratic governor vetoed the compact amid fears it could diminish his small state's outsized influence over presidential elections. Virginia became the most recent state to join the compact after Democrats there won a trifecta in 2025. Republicans called the move an " unconstitutional assault on our democracy ," arguing it undermines the influence of Virginia voters. One major question is whether lawmakers will prioritize the national popular vote after campaigning in 2026 on more visceral issues like lowering the cost of living. "Time will tell," Clinton Anderson, a Democratic state assemblyman in Wisconsin, told the Times. "I want to make it a priority, but it's not the thing I heard on the doors I knocked." Another question is what might happen in the courts if the compact actually kicks in. Notre Dame law professor Derek Muller has argued that the NPVIC would be unconstitutional without congressional approval — which, in his view, is required under the Constitution's Compact Clause. "It's a very real possibility that enough states join this compact," Muller told the Times. But, he added, "there will be a lot of challenges." articles.title: 民生银行的小微生意，换了一批客人
articles.summary: 11月3日，惠誉将民生银行长期外币发行人主体评级从BBB-上调至BBB，展望稳定。政府支持评级一同上调，衡量银行独立信用实力的生存力评级，维持在“bb-”。 两个评级一升一平，理由已经写明：惠誉认为，政府在国内系统重要性银行承压时提供特别支持的意愿在增强；民生自身的信用实力，得到的仍是“维持”。 这次上调，发生在一份利润继续下滑的三季报之后。 前三季度，民生营收同比增加20.45亿元，信用减值损失却多了74.29亿元，归母净利润下降14.78%，资金成本降了下来，更多的减值计提又压住了利润。 压力在零售账上尤其明显。上半年，对公分部多赚的钱补上了零售利润降额的大部分，集团税前利润仍在下降。零售贷款也在收缩，其中减得最多的，是个人小微。 不过，个人小微的收缩，只是小微生意的一面。 换到普惠口径，到9月末，民生普惠小微贷款余额同比增长约1.7%，有贷户却少了6.42万户。与此同时，法人普惠贷款余额较年初增加201.86亿元，占普惠小微贷款余额的比重由约28%升至31%。 生意还在做，贷款正在更多地流向企业法人。 曾经靠批量服务商户做大小微业务的民生，正在调整贷款投向：个人小微收缩，法人普惠增长，供应链成为新的获客入口，找到企业之后，民生在努力留下货款、工资和日常收付。 这轮调整已经改变了贷款结构。要让变化进一步落到利润上，民生既要消化仍在释放的信用风险，也要从客户身上做出更多贷款之外的生意。 省下的钱去了哪里 拆分利润表可见，前三季度，民生的利息收入减少了，利息净收入却增加了。 集团利息收入同比减少136.99亿元，利息支出减少174.35亿元。支出降得更快，两者相抵，利息净收入增加37.36亿元，撑住了营收增长。 太平洋证券分析师夏芈卬认为，上半年民生息差回升，得益于负债成本下降得比资产收益率更快：计息负债成本率同比下降39个基点，超过生息资产收益率30个基点的降幅。 放在存贷两端，就是付息降得比收息快。 到前三季度，民生净息差同比提高5个基点，至1.47%。但同一张利润表上，信用减值损失多了74.29亿元，约为利息净收入增量的两倍。 左口袋省下的钱，不够填右口袋漏掉的。 类似的情形已经持续超过一年。 2025年，民生营收增长4.82%，信用减值损失增加84.76亿元，归母净利润下降5.37%。今年第三季度单季，归母净利润降幅扩大到33.18%。 放在九家上市股份行中，民生前三季度营收增速比样本中位数低约半个百分点，归母净利润增速却低了近16个百分点，收入端获得了喘息，改善没能留在利润里。 上半年，集团信用减值损失的增量主要来自贷款：贷款和垫款减值损失同比增加59.11亿元。 再看业务分部，零售贡献了约36.5%的营收，税前利润却从上年同期的64.85亿元，降至亏损18.56亿元。 零售由盈转亏，贷款也在收缩。 上半年，个人贷款减少758.12亿元，其中个人小微减少310.80亿元，信用卡透支减少260.03亿元。两项合计占降额的四分之三。 即使缩量之后，个人小微贷款仍有5565.92亿元，约占个人贷款的35%，规模接近住房贷款。小微企业主和个体商户以个人名义借入的经营贷款，仍是民生零售账上的一大类资产。 小微对贷款缩量的影响更大，信用卡在不良存量里更突出。半年末，信用卡占个人贷款不良余额的53.3%，个人小微占28.3%。 民生管理层在三季度业绩会上表示，零售板块的小微和信用卡贷款，新生成不良均同比增加。 银行一边应对新出现的不良，一边处理旧贷款。 上半年，民生本行不良贷款生成率同比上升0.17个百分点至1.68%，同期清收处置不良贷款359.58亿元，其中84.18亿元通过证券化处置。 这些数字背后，是具体的借款人和抵押物。 民生今年发起的一单“鸿富”证券化产品，装入了1309户借款人的2615笔小微不良贷款。按未偿本息费计，近九成入池债权附带抵押。 中诚信国际在评估这笔交易时认为，房价波动会加大小微不良债权的处置难度，影响抵押物的处置价值和回收时间。 到三季末，民生集团不良贷款余额较年初仅减少0.25亿元；贷款总额增长2.04%，不良率从1.49%降至1.46%。比例的改善来自分母变大，分子几乎没动。 民生管理层表示，部分受困房企贷款仍在下迁，现金清收更难，处置损失率也有所上升，预计全年信贷成本仍有上行压力。 小微增量转向法人 信贷成本的压力要靠时间消化，客户结构的调整，已经写进了数据里。 三季末，民生本行普惠型小微企业贷款余额为6742.04亿元，约占本行贷款的15%。这个口径覆盖符合条件的企业法人和个人经营主体，从这里看，小微贷款的总盘子变化很小，变的是里面的结构。 2024年末，民生有51.48万户普惠小微贷款客户；2025年末，贷款余额增至6776.06亿元，有贷户降到44.39万户。 今年前三季度，民生有贷户进一步降至39.13万户，相近规模的一盘贷款，分布在了更少的客户身上，户均余额从约146万元升到172万元。 贷款余额靠法人一端补上：其余普惠小微贷款合计减少235.88亿元，与法人新增大体相抵，总余额只少了34.02亿元。 一端仍有庞大的存量，另一端能承接新的融资需求，小微仍是一门需要继续做的生意。 这种调整，发生在部分小微经营者生意承压的阶段。 北京大学企业大数据研究中心的三季度调查中，受访者平均营业收入同比下降19.5%，有45.6%表示没有外部融资需求，较上年同期提高3个百分点。 国务院发展研究中心金融研究所研究员王刚认为，今年政策淡化了普惠小微贷款增速须跟上各项贷款增速的要求。银行应按真实融资需求调节投放，把贷款更多投向有成长性的小微企业。 需求在分化，行业贷款总量仍在增长：三季末，全国人民币普惠小微贷款余额同比增长6.7%。民生的增量落在法人一端，价格却在往下走。 前三季度，民生新发放普惠小微贷款平均利率从上年同期的3.59%降至3.08%；普惠小微不良率较半年末回升0.10个百分点，至1.55%。 利率降了51个基点，不良率回升了10个基点，贷款做出去之后能留下多少收益，要重新计算。银行更需要控制资金、服务和风险成本。 招联首席经济学家董希淼认为，小微信贷要做得下去，利息收入得覆盖资金成本、运营开支和预期信用损失，定价要跟着客户的风险水平走。 民生较早就开始从获客和服务环节省钱。 做“商贷通”时，它借商圈和行业协会成批找到商户，再用标准化流程提供贷款，把逐户开发的成本，摊到更多业务上。 批量服务客户的思路仍在延续，获客入口则从商圈延伸到了供应链。围绕一家核心企业，民生可以接触它的供应商和经销商，从采购、销售和回款里寻找融资需求。 企业法人还带来一条更长的业务链。企业借钱之后，要采购、付款、收账、发工资。民生需要把这些往来做下来，让同一户客户在贷款之外继续贡献收入。 借完钱以后 这条业务链的搭建，从2024年就开始了。 当年半年报披露，民生迭代供应链数据增信融资产品，平台“云数”的脱核模式落地，数据增信融资与非现金回款结算、贴现组合使用。 到2025年末，民生链上普惠贷款余额达到518亿元，年内增加188亿元。今年三季末，覆盖范围更广的供应链金融服务链上客户数较年初增长11.69%。 这条获客路径已经带来了贷款，也把银行的经营延伸到企业交易之中。 这恰好对应了民生面临的两重压力。贷款利率下降，需要从同一客户身上增加收入；新不良仍在生成，则需要更持续地跟踪客户经营和还款能力。 但一家核心企业能带来一批客户，也会让多笔贷款受到同一付款方的影响。核心企业付款变慢，上游供应商收钱变慢，银行贷款的偿还也可能跟着受影响。 因此，民生在扩大获客的同时，把风险管理往前挪。 2025年，民生在15家重点分行组建风险派驻团队，让风险经理和有权审批人在开发客户时就介入。 订单帮助银行判断企业为什么借钱，货款回收关系到企业拿什么还钱。沿供应链做小微，批量接触客户之后，还要逐户判断还款能力，持续跟踪上下游交易。 今年前三季度，“民生快贷”优化了制造业上游供应商的服务模式，下游聚焦大消费领域。 民生管理层介绍，中小企业业务会按细分客群制定服务方案，把授信和结算配在一起，并把服务对象从企业延伸到企业主和员工。风险人员也将参与客户经营的全过程。 这些安排最终要落到账户上。 一家企业借款、收账和付款都通过民生办理，银行就有机会留下日常周转资金，再提供票据、代发等服务。一户客户的经营回报，由此多了几个来源。 全行报表已经能看到低成本负债的价值。 上半年，民生存款付息率同比下降40个基点至1.46%。到三季末，对公存款中普通活期存款占比较年初提高1.43个百分点，存款在负债中的比重提高2.55个百分点。 收入端也有一项贴近交易的变化：上半年，集团结算与清算手续费收入15.15亿元，同比增加0.82亿元。 民生已披露链上普惠贷款的规模。新获客群有多少货款和日常收付留在行内、带来了多少存款和结算收入，公开披露还没有单列。 对这家靠小微建立特色的银行来说，接下来的经营重心，是把更多借款人变成持续往来的客户。放贷只是第一次握手，账户、结算和回款才是过日子。 信用成本逐渐降下来，贷款之外的收入积累起来，这轮调整才会更多地体现在利润上。 风险提示及免责条款 articles.title: 民主党大胜，AI数据中心的输家叙事里藏着谁的机会？
articles.summary: 美国中期选举结果让AI数据中心再次站到政策争议的风口。居民电价、电网扩容和社区反对，可能使新建项目面临更严格的审批。但当公共电网越来越难以满足数据中心建设需求，企业自行解决电力供应的意愿也会增强。即使数据中心建设总量放缓，自备电渗透率仍有机会提高，现场发电设备与既有电力接入资产可能迎来新的价值重估。 一、发生了什么？——民主党大胜，AI数据中心为何突然成为输家？ 1. 一场选举，改变了市场对AI基础设施的预期： 美国2026年中期选举出现了超出此前预期的民主党胜利。美联社已报道民主党赢得众议院和参议院控制权；在得州，民主党候选人Gina Hinojosa击败Greg Abbott，当选州长。这一结果尤其值得关注：得州长期是数据中心、比特币矿场和大型能源项目的重要聚集地，而Hinojosa竞选期间明确反对能源消耗巨大的数据中心，并提出暂停新建项目、等待州议会建立新的保护机制。 市场担忧由此集中到一个问题：未来数据中心项目是否会面临更严格的选址、环保、用水和电力接入审查？地方审批趋严可能拉长建设周期，也可能让部分项目重新评估选址和供电方案。但需要区分，联邦国会控制权变化并不等于全国立即实施数据中心禁令；真正决定项目进度的，往往是州政府、地方政府、公用事业监管机构和具体许可程序。 ……

articles.title: 马斯克再抛惊人目标：明年SpaceX年化收入5000亿美元、Terafab芯片产能一太瓦、星链计算机同步上天
articles.summary: 马斯克又给AI产业描绘了一幅惊人的增长蓝图。 当地时间周五，第33届Baron Investment Conference（巴伦投资大会）举行虚拟炉边访谈，时长约七十分钟。主持人为Baron Capital创始人Ron Baron，埃隆·马斯克远程连线出席。 在访谈中，马斯克给出一系列重磅预测： SpaceX今年12月年化收入预计突破1000亿美元，明年12月年化经常性收入有望超5000亿美元；Terafab目标年产一太瓦芯片，相当于明年全球AI芯片产量的30倍；与英伟达联合设计的星链计算机预计2027年三季度开始入轨；智能体互联网流量已超人类流量，五年内或达人类流量1000倍。 SpaceX收入：从1000亿到5000亿，只用一年 SpaceX是本场访谈最受市场关注的核心对象。马斯克在访谈中明确给出了两档收入指引： " 我们正朝着12月实现年化收入超过1000亿美元的目标迈进。 显然，12月已经很近了，所以我对这一点很有把握。除非发生某种自然灾害之类的情况，我们会达到那个目标。" 更进一步，他对明年的预期同样乐观： "然后根据我们明年的计划，明年12月的年化经常性收入超过5000亿美元，这看起来很有可能。这不是承诺，这只是我认为会发生的事。 " 至于1万亿美元年化收入，马斯克说： "1万亿美元并非不可能 ，以前是不可能的，但现在不再是完全不可能了，也许有2%左右的可能性。但有意思的是，它不是0%。这才是关键。而且这个概率随着时间在增加。" SpaceX去年收入约150亿至160亿美元。若上述路径成真，这意味着不到两年时间年化收入规模将扩大逾30倍。 Terafab：明年年产全球30倍的AI芯片 马斯克在访谈中详细阐述了xAI主导推进的Terafab（太瓦工厂）计划。 他解释了命名逻辑："当我说太瓦工厂时，有时人们认为太瓦工厂有三种可能的含义：一种是吓人——TERROR，然后是TERRA，是指地球，但它实际上是TERA，即太瓦。但可以说，这三种含义都适用。" 规模上，Terafab的目标是每年产出对应一太瓦的芯片。而据马斯克预测，明年全球AI芯片总产量约为35至45吉瓦——这意味着Terafab单厂产能约为届时全球年产量的 30倍 。 马斯克指出，现有芯片制造效率存在巨大改进空间，他以一个细节说明："现在，芯片厂里一片晶圆仅仅花在运输和等待上的时间就超过一半……有时真正让原子发生有用变化的时间仅约20%。" 他的解法是在奥斯汀建研究晶圆厂，尝试将设计、制造、测试集中在同一屋檐下，"我认为我们或许能把通常需要一年的事情缩短到一个月"。背后的逻辑是："对于任何给定的技术事业来说，进步的速度取决于你能做多少次迭代……只要你有能力以数量级更快的速度迭代，大致来看，你的技术进步也会以数量级更快。" 太空算力：首批星链计算机明年发射 马斯克在访谈中多次将太空算力定位为战略级资产，逻辑链条清晰。 在他看来，地面算力扩张受制于电力：美国平均用电量刚超500吉瓦，"如果你每年建造200吉瓦的AI，那就相当于每年让整个美国电网增加40%。这根本不可行。" 太空的优势则在于持续日照、无大气衰减——太阳能利用率可额外提升约30%，且几乎无需大容量储能。"一旦你有了很低的每吨入轨成本，太空中的智能成本会比地面低得多。" 马斯克透露，目前已在发射的卫星上搭载了英伟达GPU和谷歌TPU进行测试，"据我们所知，它们在太空中运行良好"。 与英伟达共同设计的首批星链计算机预计2027年第三季度开始发射，2028年提升至可观规模，2029年达到"非常大的规模"。 他进一步给出了收入推算： "如果我们每年向太空部署100吉瓦的AI算力，每吉瓦算力的价值哪怕降到10美元，一年就是一万亿美元。而且是累积的，每年都会再增加一万亿美元，因为卫星不会蒸发。" 如果单价为50美元，则是每年5万亿美元。 马斯克预测，若每年向太空输送一太瓦的算力，相当于每年送入太空的数字超级智能是美国当前平均用电量的两倍。 星链：带宽百倍增长，智能体流量将是人类的1000倍 马斯克透露，目前约有11000颗星链卫星在轨，主要为V2版本，V3卫星刚刚开始发射。 V3相比V2能力提升超过10倍，且发射数量也将是10倍，"星链在未来两三年内产生的带宽将是目前提供的100倍"。 驱动需求的关键变量是AI智能体。 马斯克称："我的理解是，事实上智能体互联网流量已经超过了人类流量，如果我从Cloudflare的数据中读得没错的话。而且我相信Cloudflare的预测，五年内，智能体AI流量将是人类流量的一千倍。而且我认为，这甚至低估了智能体AI流量的规模。" 数据中心：350亿投入，一年回收500亿 马斯克介绍了xAI数据中心的商业逻辑：自建速度约8至9个月，远快于外部承建商的两年半；投入约350亿美元，低于市场水平。 "我们会在自己的Grok用得上之前先把算力租出去， 一年大概收500亿。350亿的投资，一年拿回500亿。" 他还透露，xAI在孟菲斯数据中心建设期间建了一座超一吉瓦的内部发电厂，"用时大约是正常建造这类设施的五分之一——大约一年建成，而通常需要五年左右"，并透露自己曾亲自参与电缆铺设、光纤接线和电气安装。 今年二季度至三季度收入增长超过80%，三至四季度预计约为70%。 人形机器人与AI对经济的影响 马斯克估计，数字超级智能将使全球经济增加约20%至30%，折合约25万亿美元，"而且这会非常快地发生"，并可能使白领工作生产力翻倍。 在物理AI方面，他给出了机器人替代劳动力的初步测算：一个高效人形机器人可近似每周工作168小时，最低生产力预期约为人的五倍；"粗略估算，约2000万至3000万个机器人可匹配美国商品和服务的产出"。商业模式上，他倾向于出租而非销售。 关于OpenAI 马斯克再度就OpenAI表态，言辞直接："我确实创办了OpenAI，作为一个开源非营利组织。现在它却是一个封闭的、追求最大利润的实体，这跟我当初创办的完全相反。" 他表示，当初并未预料到OpenAI有一天会转为营利性公司，并对非营利组织中持有商业利益的结构感到困惑："我当时很困惑，你怎么能在一家非营利组织里拥有商业利益。这在我看来说不通。" articles.title: 德州大翻车！蓝潮压境下，AI算力如何重新定价？
articles.summary: 尽管目前美国中期选举开票尚未结束，但选情已基本尘埃落定：民主党横扫国会（蓝潮），共和党惨败。截至目前，民主、共和两党在参众两院席位分别为54:43、229:135，民主党在国会席位均已过半。 此次中期选举不仅使多个关键摇摆州全部翻蓝，连德克萨斯、堪萨斯、南卡罗来纳、俄亥俄及爱荷华等传统共和党深红铁票仓也被民主党逆转。特别是德州，民主党候选人历史性击败共和党资深政客，打破共和党在该州长达30多年的绝对统治。 计票初期，蓝潮预期升温曾压制AI相关风险资产；但随着选举靴子落地，市场风险偏好回归，美股股指期货、日经225和韩国KOSPI指数由跌转涨。标普500与纳斯达克100期货在波动后回涨。亚太市场波动更为剧烈：MSCI亚太指数盘中跌超2%后收窄，日经225指数一度跌逾4.8%后反弹，韩国KOSPI由盘初下跌4%转涨，三星电子、SK海力士等芯片股跌幅收敛。清洁能源和太阳能相关标的受益于民主党政策预期。 AI产业链从算力稀缺转向许可稀缺 正如我们在11月2日《 铁票仓松动！数据中心成压垮特朗普中期选举的重要稻草？ 》中提醒，“中期选举前，由于政策走向不明及蓝潮风险，资金通常选择避险观望，市场…呈现横盘或震荡下跌的最后一跌特征。但…中期选举也是消除宏观不确定性的强催化剂。加上近期市场已部分定价中期选举蓝潮可能带来的监管收紧风险…本次选举靴子落地后，市场有较大概率重演利空出尽的反弹行情。”

articles.title: 被年轻人遗忘的磁带，正在 AI 时代闷声发大财
articles.summary: 谁能想到，磁带竟然在 AI 时代迎来了第二春。 10 月 29 日，日本富士胶片宣布投资约 100 亿日元（约合人民币 4.22 亿元），计划在 2026 至 2028 财年扩建神奈川县小田原工厂，将数据存储磁带的产能提升至 2025 财年的五倍，重点生产最新一代 LTO Ultrium 10 磁带。 按照富士胶片的说法，这是近 20 年来针对 LTO 磁带专用设施规模最大的一笔投资，而推动扩产的主要原因，正是生成式 AI 带来的海量数据归档需求。 AI 都用上了最先进的芯片，为什么还需要磁带？ 计算机行业流传着一个经典玩笑。 计算机科学家安德鲁·坦嫩鲍姆曾说过，永远不要低估一辆满载磁带、在高速公路上飞驰的汽车的带宽。听起来有些荒诞，但当需要传输的数据达到 PB 甚至 EB 级别时，把存储设备装上卡车，确实可能比通过网络传输更有效率。 2016 年，亚马逊 AWS 就曾推出 Snowmobile 服务，直接用重型卡车运输大型存储设备，一次最多可以搬运 100PB 数据。 虽然 Snowmobile 运输的并非磁带，而且该服务已于 2024 年停用，但它说明了一个长期存在的问题。当数据规模大到一定程度，如何以合理成本保存和搬运数据，本身就是一项工程挑战。 生成式 AI 的爆发，让这个问题越来越突出。 训练大模型需要 GPU、HBM 和高速 SSD，但训练结束后，企业还会留下原始语料、清洗后的数据集、训练日志、模型检查点，以及不断迭代产生的历史版本。 其中，正在参与计算的数据需要高速存储设备，经常访问的大规模数据集可以放在机械硬盘上，而那些几个月甚至几年都用不到、却又不能随便删除的资料，则适合进入长期归档系统。 行业通常将访问频率很低的数据称为冷数据。 例如，一家 AI 公司训练完新模型，旧版数据集短期内可能已经没有用途，但未来复现实验、重新训练或者进行合规审计时，仍然可能需要重新调用。 问题随之而来。当数据越积越多，难道要让所有硬盘一直通电，花钱维护那些可能几年都不会访问一次的文件？ 磁带恰好擅长做这件事。 首先是便宜，而且省电。磁带可以长期离线保存，闲置时无需持续供电，也不需要像在线硬盘阵列那样维持设备运行和散热。 富士胶片曾测算，在保存 100PB 数据、周期为十年的特定条件下，自动化磁带系统相比全机械硬盘方案，可以降低约 86% 的总体拥有成本，以及约 95% 的碳排放。 其次是安全。磁带能够从系统中取出并离线保存，即使服务器遭到勒索软件攻击，物理隔离的磁带仍有机会保留一份独立备份。 而且，现代磁带也没有想象中那么慢。LTO-10 的原始连续传输速率最高可达 1200MB/s，自动化磁带库还能利用机械手完成装载和读取。 不过，磁带需要顺序寻找数据，随机读取一个文件可能需要较长时间，因此不适合频繁访问和实时计算。如果说 AI 数据中心的 SSD 负责让数据随叫随到，那么磁带更像一座成本低廉、容量庞大的数字仓库。 事实上，科学界早就在使用这种方案。 2025 年 12 月，欧洲核子研究中心 CERN 宣布，大型强子对撞机累计保存的实验数据达到 1EB，相当于 100 万 TB，其中大部分数据保存在约 6 万盒磁带上。 几十年前采集的实验数据，可能因为新理论的出现而重新获得研究价值。CERN 预计，未来十年需要保存和处理的数据规模，将达到此前累计存储量的约十倍。 类似的逻辑，也适用于 AI 企业保存的历史语料、训练记录和模型备份。 而磁带市场的增长，已经有实际数据支撑。 根据 LTO 联盟 2026 年 9 月公布的数据，2024 年全球 LTO 磁带出货容量达到创纪录的 176.5EB，同比增长 15.4%。2025 年虽然有所回落，仍达到 160.3EB。 进入 2026 年第一季度，随着 LTO-10 上市及归档需求增长，全球磁带出货容量又同比增长 57%。这里统计的是磁带所提供的存储容量，并非磁带盒销量。 企业级磁带一直拥有稳定市场，而生成式 AI 对海量数据归档的需求，又让这项老技术获得了新的增长机会。 一盒磁带能存100TB，26年容量暴涨400倍 磁带能在 AI 时代重新获得关注，还有一个容易被忽略的原因。 当普通消费者以为磁带技术早已停滞时，工程师其实一直在提高它的存储密度。 2025 年 6 月，富士胶片推出 LTO-10 30TB 数据磁带，同年 12 月又发布 40TB 版本，并于 2026 年开始供货。最新产品的单盒原始容量达到 40TB，如果按照理想条件下 2.5:1 的压缩比计算，理论容量最高可以达到 100TB。 图｜LTO-10 30TB 作为对比，2000 年推出的第一代 LTO 磁带，原始容量只有 100GB。短短 26 年，单盒容量足足提高了 400 倍。不过，100TB 是理论压缩容量，对于已经压缩过的视频、图片和模型权重，实际容量通常无法达到这个数字。 更有意思的是，LTO-10 磁带盒只有约 10 厘米见方、2.15 厘米厚，内部却卷着长达 1337 米的磁带，相当于三圈多标准田径跑道。 为了将长达 1337 米的磁带装进一盒仅约 10 厘米见方的卡带，富士胶片引入芳纶薄膜和新型薄层制造技术，将磁带整体厚度降低至仅 4 微米，同时采用结合钡铁氧体与锶铁氧体技术的超细磁性颗粒，提高单位面积能够记录的数据量。 至于存储原理，其实与几十年前的录音磁带一脉相承。 磁带表面覆盖着微小的磁性颗粒，写入数据时，磁头通过改变局部磁化状态记录数字信息；读取时，再检测磁场变化，通过解码和纠错还原数据。 现代 LTO 磁带采用线性蛇形记录方式，可以把它想象成一条拥有上万条车道的公路。磁头沿一组磁道从头写到尾，再调整位置反方向写回来。 最新 LTO-10 拥有 15104 条数据磁道，驱动器可同时读写 32 条磁道，依靠更精密的材料和伺服控制技术不断提高容量。 而且，磁带的容量增长远没有到头。 2020 年，IBM 与富士胶片就曾在实验室实现每平方英寸 317Gb 的磁记录密度，展示了未来单盒磁带达到 580TB 的技术潜力，相当于目前 40TB 商用产品的 14.5 倍。 当然，580TB 仍停留在实验室演示阶段，距离商业化还有很长一段路。 磁带还有一项经常被忽视的长期成本，那就是兼容性。 磁带介质可以保存很多年，却不意味着几十年后的新驱动器依然能够读取它。最新 LTO-10 驱动器只能读写 LTO-10 磁带，企业需要保留旧设备，或者定期将历史数据迁移到新介质。 对于管理数万盒磁带的数据中心而言，数据迁移、校验和设备维护同样是一笔不小的开支。 即便如此，在大规模冷数据归档场景中，磁带依然拥有很强的成本和能耗竞争力。富士胶片过去几十年积累的精密涂布、薄膜材料和磁性颗粒技术，也因此在 AI 时代重新获得商业价值。 磁带的故事，在机械硬盘行业同样上演。 今年 1 月，西部数据透露，公司 2026 日历年的硬盘产能基本售罄，部分大型客户的长期采购协议已经延伸至 2028 年。 希捷的情况更加夸张。根据 10 月下旬的财报电话会议，公司绝大部分近线机械硬盘出货容量已通过长期协议分配至 2028 年，部分云服务商的采购协议甚至覆盖到 2030 年。 更值得关注的是，机械硬盘不光卖得多，价格也在上涨。 原因并不复杂。SSD 的随机读写性能远超机械硬盘，但对于需要长期在线保存海量数据的云服务商而言，机械硬盘依然拥有每 TB 成本优势。 尤其是 AI 产业持续扩张，训练数据、模型文件和各类生成内容不断累积，数据中心需要的不只有更快的 SSD，还有能够以合理价格提供数十 PB、数百 PB 容量的机械硬盘。 当然，HDD 也存在性能和维护成本。随着单盘容量不断增加，随机访问能力并不会同比提高，故障后的数据重建时间也可能拉长。 但对于云服务商而言，只要存储成本、容量密度和访问性能能够满足业务需求，机械硬盘就依然有存在的价值。 从富士胶片宣布五倍扩产，到西部数据全年产能基本售罄，再到希捷与云服务商签订延伸至 2030 年的长期协议，一批在消费电子市场逐渐失去存在感的传统技术，正在 AI 数据中心找到新的增长空间。 不过，磁带未来也可能迎来新的竞争者。 2026 年 2 月，微软研究院在《Nature》发表 Project Silica 的最新成果，研究人员利用飞秒激光将数据写入玻璃内部，在约 12 厘米见方、2 毫米厚的玻璃中实现了 4.8TB 的存储容量。 根据加速老化测试，研究人员推算，数据有望保存超过一万年。虽然距离大规模商业应用仍有距离，却展示了长期归档的另一种可能性。 某种程度上，AI 时代的数据存储正在呈现出一幅颇为奇妙的画面。 一边，富士胶片还在改进延续几十年的磁粉涂布工艺，让小小一盒磁带装下数十 TB 数据；另一边，微软已经开始尝试像远古人类在石头上刻字一样，用激光把信息写进玻璃。 当全世界都在追逐更强大的 GPU、更聪明的大模型时，那些负责保存数据的老技术，反倒迎来了属于自己的黄金时代。 风口从来不只属于新事物，也属于那些在新风口里找到自己位置的老手艺。 本文来源： APPSO 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。

articles.title: Arista财报解读：为什么它交出了不一样的答卷？
articles.summary: 当"AI 硬件股"在一周内被市场系统性下调估值时，一家交换机公司用一份"指引高于共识12.8%"的财报，把盘后股价推高了12%。高盛统计，这是本轮AI调整行情中第一次出现业绩与股价脱钩，Arista是那个显著的例外。它由三个结构性错配造成的。 第一，市场把Arista当作"AI 资本开支的高贝塔代理"，但它2026年AI收入占比只有26.3%，三成以上的收入来自与AI无关的园区与传统云网络。 第二，市场焦虑的核心已从"需求是否存在"切换到"建设资金从哪来"，而Arista恰好是整条产业链上唯一不消耗资本的公司——资本开支仅占收入1.3%，账上143.59亿美元现金且无有息负债，非常健康。 第三，市场用44倍的滚动市盈率为它定价，而按公司自己的2027年指引与49%营业利润率推算，隐含市盈率约为30倍前瞻盈利。

articles.title: Apollo拟豪掷750亿美元采购AI芯片，规模远超任何一家Neocloud
articles.summary: 私募巨头Apollo Global Management正以前所未有的规模押注AI芯片市场，其两笔待完成的芯片交易合计金额高达750亿美元，不仅远超最大neocloud CoreWeave自2023年以来累计270亿美元的芯片融资规模，更是排名第二的竞争对手的逾10倍。 据The Information最新报道， SpaceX宣布将租用价值400亿美元的英伟达Vera Rubin芯片，而Apollo将通过旗下子公司购入这批芯片后再租赁给SpaceX。 此前，Apollo已于今年6月宣布联合Broadcom与Blackstone，为其购买谷歌张量处理器（TPU）并租赁给Anthropic的交易安排了350亿美元融资。 一旦上述交易完成，在AI芯片持有规模上， Apollo将仅次于亚马逊、微软、谷歌等超大规模云服务商，成为全球芯片储备最雄厚的非超大规模玩家 ，彻底改变AI基础设施的竞争格局。Apollo在这些交易中通过撮合交易及管理融资基金赚取费用。 两笔巨型交易奠定芯片霸主地位 Apollo当前的芯片布局由两笔核心交易构成。 其一是今年6月宣布的350亿美元交易： Apollo联合Broadcom与Blackstone，购买谷歌TPU并租赁给AI初创公司Anthropic。 其二是上周随SpaceX公告浮出水面的400亿美元交易： Apollo通过子公司购入英伟达Vera Rubin芯片，再租赁给马斯克旗下的SpaceX。 两笔交易合计750亿美元，使Apollo在芯片融资领域的体量远超任何一家neocloud。据The Information汇编的数据，CoreWeave自2023年以来通过芯片抵押融资累计筹资270亿美元，位居neocloud之首；其后依次为Valor（54亿美元）、Nscale（49亿美元）、IREN（39亿美元）、Lambda（15亿美元）、Crusoe（11亿美元）、Nebius（7.75亿美元）及Sharon AI（3.56亿美元）。 值得注意的是，上述统计仅涵盖以GPU和TPU为抵押的融资，不包括各家neocloud为运营融资而发行的可转换债券及信贷额度。此外，上周另有一笔由花旗集团、美国银行与Blackstone联合安排、规模达630亿美元的交易——用于为Anthropic采购Broadcom芯片提供融资——亦未纳入上述比较，原因是各方未披露这批芯片的实际持有方。 芯片融资模式：SPV结构的规模化复制 Apollo所采用的芯片融资结构，脱胎于CoreWeave与Blackstone在2023年共同开创的特殊目的载体（SPV）模式。 在这一安排下，neocloud与其金融合作方共同设立SPV，由SPV发行债务以购买芯片，芯片终端用户支付的租金则用于偿还债务。 Apollo的操作逻辑与此一脉相承，但规模更为庞大。与许多neocloud不同的是，Apollo并未额外投入资本建设用于存放芯片的数据中心，其商业模式更为聚焦——通过购买芯片、出租给终端用户，赚取交易撮合费用及基金管理费。 超大规模云服务商则无需借助SPV结构，可直接通过自由现金流、股权发行或传统公司债完成芯片采购，这也是Apollo与超大规模云服务商之间的本质区别。 保险资本驱动Apollo转型 Apollo的芯片豪赌，折射出这家老牌私募机构过去十年的深刻转型。Apollo由亿万富翁Leon Black联合创立，成立已逾36年，早年以杠杆收购闻名，其中包括2008年斥资近300亿美元收购赌场巨头哈拉斯娱乐。 过去十年间，Apollo大规模吸纳来自保险公司的资本。保险资金偏好收益率高于投资级债券、但信用评级仍维持投资级的资产类别，而芯片融资交易恰好契合这一需求。 这一资本结构的转变，为Apollo在AI基础设施领域的大规模布局提供了充裕的弹药。 芯片融资对Apollo而言是一个全新的业务方向，但其背后的逻辑与传统私募信贷如出一辙：以资产为抵押，提供结构化融资，赚取稳定的利差收益。随着AI算力需求持续膨胀，Apollo正将这一逻辑推向新的量级。 风险提示及免责条款 市场有风险，投资需谨慎。本文不构成个人投资建议，也未考虑到个别用户特殊的投资目标、财务状况或需要。用户应考虑本文中的任何意见、观点或结论是否符合其特定状况。据此投资，责任自负。
